---
title: ArkType
---

ArkType parses its regex literals with ArkRegex, so they're inferred without any extra setup:

```ts
const Semver = type("/^(\\d+)\\.(\\d+)\\.(\\d+)$/")
//    ^?
```

A `Regex` instance can also be used directly as a definition:

```ts
const Package = type({
	name: "string",
	version: regex("^(\\d+)\\.(\\d+)\\.(\\d+)$")
})

type Package = typeof Package.infer
//   ^?
```

## e(x)ec mode

Prefix a regex literal with `x` to parse its captures as part of validation:

```ts
const User = type({
	birthday: "x/^(?<month>\\d{2})-(?<day>\\d{2})-(?<year>\\d{4})$/"
})

const data = User.assert({ birthday: "05-21-1993" })

data.birthday.groups.month // "05"
//                   ^?
```

See [string patterns](/docs/primitives#string-patterns) for more on regex literals in ArkType.


---
title: Errors
---

Anything `new RegExp()` would throw on is a type error, as are some patterns that are valid but almost certainly mistakes.

```ts
// @errors: 2345
regex("^(a)\\2$")

regex("^(?<a>x)\\k<b>$")

regex("a(b")

regex("+a")
```

## Escapes

Escaping a character with no special meaning is an error, as is double-escaping a character JS strings can already represent:

```ts
// @errors: 2345
regex("\\q")

regex("\\n")
```

## Escape hatch

If you need to bypass validation, use [`regex.as`](/docs/regex/types#regexas).


---
title: FAQ
---

### Why aren't some patterns like `[a-Z]` inferred more precisely?

Constructing string literal types for these sorts of expressions is combinatorial and will explode very quickly if we infer character ranges like this as literal characters.

We've tried to strike a balance between performance and precision while guaranteeing that the inferred types are at worst imprecise and never incorrect.

### Why doesn't it work with my massive RegExp?

If your expression is especially long or complex, TypeScript won't be able to infer it.

If your types start to slow down or you see the dreaded `Type instantiation is excessively deep...`, you can manually type your expression using [`regex.as`](/docs/regex/types#regexas).

### Is it robust?

`arkregex` types are [extensively tested](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/tree/main/ark/regex/__tests__/regex.test.ts) and [benchmarked](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/tree/main/ark/regex/__tests__/regex.bench.ts) using [Attest](/docs/attest).

If anything isn't behaving how you'd expect, please don't hesitate to [create an issue](https://github.com/arktypeio/arktype/issues/new).


---
title: Setup
---

ArkRegex is a drop-in replacement for `new RegExp()` with types.

The `regex` function creates a `Regex` instance with types for `.test()`, `.exec()` and more, statically parsed from native JS syntax:

```ts
import { regex } from "arkregex"

const ok = regex("^ok$", "i")
//    ^?

const semver = regex("^(\\d+)\\.(\\d+)\\.(\\d+)$")
//    ^?

const email = regex("^(?<name>\\w+)@(?<domain>\\w+\\.\\w+)$")
//    ^?
```

At runtime, `regex(src, flags)` is just `new RegExp(src, flags)`, so it adds nothing to your bundle beyond a single function.

## Installation

<InstallationTabs pkg="arkregex" />

Performs best with TypeScript 5.9+.

## Features

- **Types**: Infers string types for your existing regular expressions, including positional and named captures
- **Parity**: Supports 100% of [features](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide/Regular_expressions) allowed by `new RegExp()`
- **Safety**: Syntax errors like referencing a group that doesn't exist are now [type errors](/docs/regex/errors)
- **Zero Runtime**: Improves your type safety without impacting your bundle size

## Syntax highlighting

The [ArkType extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=arktypeio.arkdark) adds syntax highlighting to `regex` calls.

## ArkType

ArkType uses ArkRegex to infer its own regex literals, so `type("/^\\d+$/")` is already typed. See [ArkType integration](/docs/regex/arktype).


---
title: Inference
---

Each `Regex` carries the type of string it matches along with any captures and flags.

Inferred types are at worst imprecise and never incorrect: anything ArkRegex can't represent as a literal widens to `string` or `${number}`.

## Anchors

An expression without `^` or `$` can match anywhere in a string, so its type is padded with `${string}`:

```ts
const unanchored = regex("abc")
//    ^?

const anchored = regex("^abc$")
//    ^?
```

## Unions

```ts
const color = regex("^(red|green|blue)$")
//    ^?
```

## Quantifiers

Bounded quantifiers are expanded when the result is small:

```ts
const range = regex("^a{2,3}$")
//    ^?

const optional = regex("^colou?r$")
//    ^?
```

Unbounded repetition of a digit becomes `${number}`:

```ts
const version = regex("^(\\d+)\\.(\\d+)$")
//    ^?
```

## Character sets

Small sets become unions of literals. Ranges like `[a-z]` would quickly produce enormous unions, so they widen to `string`:

```ts
const abc = regex("^[abc]$")
//    ^?

const hex = regex("^[0-9a-f]+$")
//    ^?
```

## Captures

Positional captures are inferred as a tuple, and correlate with each branch of a union:

```ts
const color = regex("^(red|green|blue)$")

type Captures = typeof color.inferCaptures
//   ^?
```

A group that may not participate in a match captures `undefined`:

```ts
const optional = regex("^a(b)?$")
//    ^?
```

## Named captures

```ts
const date = regex("^(?<year>\\d{4})-(?<month>\\d{2})-(?<day>\\d{2})$")

type Names = typeof date.inferNamedCaptures
//   ^?
```

## Flags

Flags are inferred, and `i` expands case-insensitive literals:

```ts
const ok = regex("^ok$", "i")
//    ^?
```

## `.test()`

`.test()` narrows its input to the expression's type:

```ts
const color = regex("^(red|green|blue)$")

const parse = (s: string) => {
	if (color.test(s)) return s
	//                        ^?
	return null
}
```

## `.exec()`

`.exec()` returns a fully typed result, including `groups` and, with the `d` flag, `indices`:

```ts
const date = regex("^(?<year>\\d{4})-(?<month>\\d{2})-(?<day>\\d{2})$", "d")

const result = date.exec("2026-10-07")

if (result) {
	result.groups.year
	//            ^?
	result.indices.groups.year
	//                    ^?
}
```


---
title: Types
---

## `Regex`

`Regex<pattern, ctx>` extends `RegExp`, so it can be passed anywhere a `RegExp` is expected.

Its type parameters can be extracted from an instance:

```ts
const date = regex("^(?<year>\\d{4})-(?<month>\\d{2})$")

type Pattern = typeof date.infer
//   ^?

type Captures = typeof date.inferCaptures
//   ^?

type Names = typeof date.inferNamedCaptures
//   ^?
```

Or used to constrain one:

```ts
import type { Regex } from "arkregex"

const parseVersion = (r: Regex<`${number}.${number}`>) => {}

parseVersion(regex("^(\\d+)\\.(\\d+)$"))
```

## `regex.infer`

Infers the pattern of an expression without creating an instance:

```ts
import { regex } from "arkregex"

type Version = regex.infer<"^(\\d+)\\.(\\d+)$">
//   ^?
```

`regex.parse` gives you the full `Regex` type, and `regex.validate` the parameter type `regex` uses to report errors, so you can write your own wrappers:

```ts
import { regex } from "arkregex"

const anchored = <src extends string>(
	src: regex.validate<src>
): regex.parse<`^${src}$`> => regex.as(`^${src}$`) as never

const ab = anchored("a(b)")
//    ^?
```

## `regex.as`

If an expression is too long or complex for TypeScript to infer (e.g. you see `Type instantiation is excessively deep`), you can type it manually with `regex.as`. It skips parsing and validation entirely:

```ts
const complexPattern = regex.as<`pattern-${string}`, { captures: [string] }>(
	"very-long-complex-expression-here"
)
```
